chapters.title: Chapter 2: Trend, Support and Resistance on Currency Pairs

lessons.title: Multi-Timeframe Analysis: Aligning the Daily Trend With Intraday Entries

children.text: Sneha day-trades USD/INR futures on NSE, and she only ever looks at the 15-minute chart. When it dips, she shorts. When it rises, she goes long. Over the past month she has been stopped out far more often than she has won, even though the pair has been in a clean, obvious uptrend on the daily chart the entire time. Every one of her losing shorts was a pullback within that uptrend, not a reversal, and the 15-minute chart alone never told her the difference.

body.text: Let the higher timeframe decide the direction you are allowed to trade, and use the lower timeframe only to time your entry within that direction. On global spot pairs, add the session filter from Chapter 1 on top: the identical low-timeframe signal deserves more trust during an overlap than during a thin session.

children.text: Multi-timeframe analysis simply means checking more than one chart before you act, in a fixed order, so that a shorter timeframe never overrides what a longer one is telling you about the underlying trend.

body.title: The top-down checklist, before every entry
steps: Read the daily chart first. Use the trendline and moving average tools from the last lesson to decide whether the pair is in an uptrend, a downtrend, or no clear trend at all. This is your bias, and it does not change every few hours.
Move to a middle timeframe, typically 1-hour. Find where price currently sits relative to the daily trend, usually a pullback toward a trendline, moving average or prior support or resistance zone.

Move to your entry timeframe, typically 15-minute or 5-minute. Wait for a confirmed candlestick signal in the direction of your daily bias, using the confirmation habits from Chapter 1, not a raw wick.
Only take the trade if all three line up: daily bias, a logical pullback level on the middle timeframe, and a confirmed trigger on the entry timeframe. If any one is missing, skip the trade.

body.caption: One setup, read across three timeframes

cells: Price above a rising trendline and above the 50-day moving average
Bias is up. Only long trades are on the table today
Price has pulled back to the rising trendline and is stalling there
This is a logical place to look for a long entry, not a random level
A bearish wick forms first, then a confirmed bullish engulfing candle closes higher
The confirmed candle, not the wick, is the actual entry trigger

body.title: Illustrative USD/INR, 15-Minute Entry Trigger at the 1-Hour Trendline

children.text: This is an illustrative pattern, not a live quote. The 10:15 am candle dips to 94.60, right into the 1-hour trendline zone, and looks bearish on its own. The 10:30 am candle is the actual signal, a large bullish body that engulfs the prior candle and closes near its high. That is the entry, confirmed by structure on two higher timeframes, not a guess taken off one 15-minute chart in isolation.

body.title: Apply the checklist
body.scenario: Arjun is looking at USD/INR futures. The daily chart shows price below a falling trendline and below its 50-day moving average, a clear downtrend. On the 1-hour chart, price has just rallied up into that falling trendline and stalled. On the 15-minute chart, a small bearish pin bar has just closed right at the trendline.
body.prompt: Using the top-down checklist, does this setup qualify for a trade, and if so, in which direction?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Daily bias is down, since price sits below both the falling trendline and the 50-day moving average. Only short trades qualify today.
2. The 1-hour chart shows price rallying into a logical resistance zone, the falling trendline, which is exactly the kind of pullback-into-resistance setup worth watching in a downtrend.
3. The 15-minute bearish pin bar closing at that trendline is a confirmed signal in the direction of the daily bias, not against it.
4. All three line up: downtrend bias, a logical resistance level on the 1-hour chart, and a confirmed bearish trigger on the 15-minute chart. This qualifies as a short entry near the trendline, with a stop placed above the recent 1-hour high.

children.text: Timeframe Conflict: What to Do When They Disagree

A daily uptrend will regularly produce short-term downward moves on the 15-minute chart. That is not a conflict to resolve, it is simply what a pullback looks like up close. The rule is one-directional: the higher timeframe decides what direction you are allowed to trade, full stop. A lower-timeframe move against that bias is either a pullback to buy into, or a reason to stand aside, never a standalone reason to trade against the daily trend.

body.title: Reading a short-term move against the daily trend
body.question: The daily chart shows a clear, well-established uptrend. On the 15-minute chart, price drops sharply and a bearish engulfing candle closes lower. What is the most disciplined response?
options: Short immediately, since the 15-minute chart just gave a clear bearish signal
Treat the drop as a possible pullback within the uptrend and look for a bullish entry trigger once it stalls at a logical support level
Ignore both charts and check a weekly chart instead
Average down on an existing short position
body.explanation: The daily uptrend sets the only direction worth trading. A bearish 15-minute candle inside that uptrend is far more likely to be a pullback than a genuine reversal, so the disciplined move is to wait for it to reach a logical support level and look for a confirmed bullish trigger there, not to fight the higher timeframe.

children.text: Adding the Session Filter for Global Pairs

On EUR/USD and other global spot pairs, the top-down checklist needs one extra filter you already have from Chapter 1. A confirmed 15-minute trigger that lines up perfectly with your daily bias and your 1-hour pullback level still deserves less trust if it fires at 3:00 am IST, in the Sydney-only window, than if the identical setup fires at 7:00 pm IST, inside the London-New York overlap. Timeframe alignment tells you the setup is structurally sound. The session tells you whether real volume is actually behind it right now.

body.text: This is not a separate rule so much as the two ideas from this course stacking together. A structurally aligned setup during a high-liquidity overlap is the strongest kind of entry you can find on a global spot pair. The same structure during a thin session is a setup to note and wait on, not one to size up and trade immediately.

body.title: Two filters, not one
body.textWithBlank: On a global spot pair, a trade should ideally pass two checks before entry: alignment across the daily, middle and entry timeframes, and confirmation that the entry candle formed during a period of genuine ___.
body.explanation: Timeframe alignment confirms the setup is structurally sound. A high-liquidity session or overlap confirms real volume is behind the signal, not thin-market noise.

cards.definition: The trade direction allowed by the higher timeframe, established before looking at any lower timeframe chart.
Checking a higher timeframe for trend direction, a middle timeframe for the current pullback level, and a lower timeframe for a confirmed entry trigger, in that order.
When a lower timeframe shows a short-term move against the higher timeframe's trend. Resolved by treating it as a pullback, not a reversal, unless the higher timeframe itself changes.
Checking whether a confirmed entry trigger on a global spot pair formed during a high-liquidity session or overlap, adding a second layer of confidence beyond timeframe alignment.

points: Read the daily chart first to set your bias, then a middle timeframe to find the current pullback level, then your entry timeframe to time a confirmed trigger. Only trade when all three line up.
A short-term move against the daily trend on a lower timeframe is usually a pullback, not a reversal. The higher timeframe decides direction, full stop.
On NSE currency futures, the same session produces the daily, 1-hour and 15-minute charts you are reading, so timeframe alignment works cleanly on its own.

On global spot pairs, add the session filter from Chapter 1: the identical aligned setup deserves more confidence during a high-liquidity overlap than during a thin session like the Sydney-only window.
Timeframe alignment confirms a setup is structurally sound. The session confirms whether real volume is actually behind it right now. Strong entries have both.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not trading advice. All chart and table examples are illustrative and not live or historical quotes. Multi-timeframe alignment reduces certain kinds of false signals but does not eliminate risk, and should be combined with proper position sizing and stop-losses before any trade.
